content: This article was originally published in LAist. A majority of students are complying with Los Angeles Unified’s cellphone ban and paying more attention in class, at least according to school staff. That’s one finding from the first survey of students and staff to include questions about bell-to-bell restrictions implemented in February 2025. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter “It’s a big difference in terms of [students’] ability and willingness to focus on whatever we’re doing in class,” said Elizabeth Ruff, an English teacher at Garfield High School. “Obviously there are always some kids who are distracted … even if it’s not their phone. But that has decreased a lot really, really markedly.” But there are still unanswered questions about what effect, if any, LAUSD’s student phone-use restrictions have on student learning and behavior, including recent gains on state tests. Compliance varies, too: Middle school staff estimated that two-thirds of students “mostly” abided by the restrictions. Among high school staff, that number dropped to just over half. More than 160,000 students answered the survey, as did more than 21,000 staff members. The results of the spring 2026 School Experience Survey, which queries staff, students and parents on a number of topics, are the first public, quantitative measure of how LAUSD’s updated cellphone policy has changed student behavior on campus. While some survey answers are available online , results of the questions specific to the cellphone policy were released to LAist only upon request. LAUSD’s policy predated the state of California’s requirements for all schools to restrict student cellphones by July 2026 . At least 40 states and the District of Columbia have similar restrictions, according to Education Week , largely based on the premise that phones and social media distract students from learning and amplify conflicts , among other concerns. How middle and high school students differ LAUSD middle and high school students are split nearly evenly on whether the policy improved their focus in class. Myson Thomas, 17, is a senior at King/Drew Magnet High School. He said he doesn’t use his school’s magnetically sealed Yondr pouches, but he also isn’t on his phone in class. “I’m at school to learn, so I’m gonna turn my phone off,” Thomas said. “I already take rigorous courses, so it’s no point of me using my phone at school.” Fewer than half of high school students reported they focused better in class all or most of the time without their phone compared to nearly 58% of their peers in middle school. Is LAUSD’s cellphone ban helping students? The annual Student Experience Survey asked more than 160,000 students for their opinions on the cellphone ban, which started in February 2025. The survey was completed by 95% of middle school students and 91% of high school students. “In implementing a phone-free policy across the district, we recognized that changing long-standing habits would take time,” a district spokesperson said in a statement to LAist. “We recognize there is still work to do and will continue listening to students, families and staff as we refine our approach to support focused learning and meaningful in-person connections.” Board Member Nick Melvoin, who co-sponsored the cellphone policy, said he was “really encouraged” that most middle and high school student respondents said they were interacting with each other more without their phones. “This isn’t just about trying to be punitive adults,” Melvoin said. “This is about [students] having a much more engaging day, a more fulfilling day when you’re not just scrolling or texting.” How we got here LAUSD joined a growing number of districts and states clamping down on student cellphone use in June 2024 when the school board voted to extend the existing class-time ban to include lunch and passing periods. Board members cited concerns about the effect of phones and social media on youth mental health , bullying and distraction from classroom instruction . Educators who spoke in support of stricter rules said their schools had few resources or administrative support to enforce the existing rules and said that policing phone use ate up time and created conflicts with students. How have LAUSD staff experienced the cellphone ban? The annual Student Experience Survey asked more than 21,000 educators for their feelings about the cellphone ban, which started in February 2025. The survey was completed by 93% of middle school staff and 92% of high school staff. “It definitely felt a little bit like playing Whac-A-Mole in terms of trying to do everything else I’m supposed to be doing in the classroom and also be looking out for who secretly has a cellphone behind their book,” said Ruff, the Garfield High School teacher. How LAUSD enforced phone restrictions The board’s vote allocated $7 million to implement the policy. Schools could choose whether they wanted to purchase pouches or lockers to store students’ phones or rely on the “honor system,” and ask students to keep their devices powered off and in their backpacks. About half of schools purchased devices to enforce the ban, according to a district spokesperson at the time the policy went into effect . Documents provided to LAist through a public records request show LAUSD spent about $6.35 million on products related to cellphone policy implementation during the 2024-25 school year. Of that, the district spent $5.42 million on Yondr products (including phone pouches) and nearly $930,000 on products from Amazon, including phone lockers. What we know about the effectiveness of phone restrictions LAist first spoke to Miles, a student at the Sherman Oaks Center for Enriched Studies, when the restrictions began in 2025. At the time, he called the phone-free policy “really, really annoying.” “I think it’s still a pretty useless policy,” Miles, now a junior, said. ”It doesn’t change anything other than how we hide our phones.” LAist agreed not to publish Miles’ last name to protect his privacy. He, like Thomas, said he doesn’t use his school’s phone storage pouches and doesn’t use his phone in class. Students have also reportedly circumvented the pouches by storing a dummy phone or breaking open the locks . However, a national study of school campuses found phone use declined when students are required to stow their phones in locking pouches. “Even though the compliance isn’t perfect, it actually still has a big impact on how many phones are being used at school,” said Matthew Gentzkow, a professor of economics at Stanford and study co-author. Related Phone Bans Improve Learning, Study Finds — But So Far, Only Slightly The study evaluated GPS data to measure phone activity at more than 40,000 schools . Gentzkow said even though the data is “imperfect” because it does not distinguish student phone use from adults on campus, the usage “falls really quite dramatically” after the pouches are introduced — there are about 30% fewer GPS pings measured three years after the ban is adopted on a campus. Yondr, the company that makes the pouches, provided the data for the study, but did not influence the findings, Gentzkow said. The study also examined disciplinary actions, student test scores, attendance data and surveys, finding: Disciplinary incidents increase in the first year a phone policy goes into effect, but decline in subsequent years. A “close to zero” effect on test scores and attendance. Student well-being takes a couple of years to improve. LAist also asked Gentzkow to respond to LAUSD’s school survey data. He noted that students were more likely to report socially interacting more with their peers without their phones than they were to focus better in class. “That dovetails with our finding that the academic benefits here, at least as measured by test scores, are maybe somewhat disappointing or somewhat smaller than we might have expected,” Gentzkow said. “Whereas things like these well-being benefits may reflect these important changes outside of the classroom as a result of these policies.” The study Gentzkow worked on is one of several that have found mixed results after schools implement stricter cellphone policies. For example, a study of Florida schools found a modest test score increase after a state-mandated cellphone ban, particularly in schools with high phone usage before the policy went into effect. LAUSD students increased their scores on the state’s standardized reading and math tests over the last three years , but those gains began before the district’s cellphone ban began. East Valley High School social studies teacher Mario Narciso said his school has used both pouches and lockers to try to curb students’ cellphone use. Even though enforcement varies on campus, he said he doesn’t see phones as a “huge problem” anymore. “At the end of the day,” he said, “it’s more about that relationship that you have with your kids.”
